title: 257 trades, +$20.5k, five weeks on a paper desk — which prop firm will actually let a bot trade this?
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Disclosure, since my username gives it away anyway: I built the platform this runs on. The bot is mine, the problem is real, and there's nothing to sell you here — you can't buy what I'm asking for.

Five weeks ago I put a bot on a paper desk to see whether an idea I'd been trading by hand would hold up when something other than me was running it. It sells defined-risk put spreads — 5% out of the money, 3% wing, about two weeks to expiry — on index ETFs and large caps, and only when relative volume is elevated and price is above its 200-day.

257 trades, 234 winners, +$20,508.

Before anyone else says it: I know exactly what a 91% win rate on credit spreads means. You win a little very often and lose a lot rarely, and five weeks is nowhere near long enough to have met that loss. The curve is smooth because the bad day hasn't happened yet, not because there isn't one. My own backtest of the same idea over two years grades it "positive, but below the bar — prove it live first." That's my own engine telling me not to trust my own bot, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

What I do trust is the fill model. It buys at the ask and sells at the bid, never the mid, and never sees a price before it existed. So the number isn't flattered by the usual backtest lies. It's just young.

Here's my actual problem. Nearly every prop firm I can find is futures or forex. This trades US equity and ETF options. So:

1. Is there any funded or prop programme that takes defined-risk equity option spreads at all?

2. Of those, which permit real automation — an API or a bridge — rather than "you may use an EA, but a human has to press the button"?

3. For anyone who has actually done this: what killed you? I assume the daily drawdown rule is the real enemy for something that holds to expiry instead of flattening intraday.

I'd genuinely rather hear "don't, and here's why" than nothing.

Free to start, and nothing anywhere asks for a card.

If you do poke at it, the thing I'd genuinely want your eyes on is the verdict, because that's the part that's easy to fake and hard to prove. Build something, grade it, and tell me whether the SHADOW and SHELF results read as honest or as a product hedging its bets. Of 177 graded strategies on the production fleet, 8 came back LIVE and 17 came back SHELF — most things land in the middle, and I'd rather that be visible than tidy.

Two things to know going in so they're not a surprise. It's paper throughout — no broker, no orders, nothing at stake but your time. And the equity curve currently sums closed trades, which means it hides the ride between entry and exit; someone in this sub caught that and it's being rebuilt. Don't trust that chart's smoothness until I've fixed it.

If it annoys you, I'd rather hear that than nothing.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
On the bot in that post — and being precise, because the grading rules make this less simple than the question sounds.

Both exist as live overlays, plus a third: a ratchet that raises a floor under a winner as it climbs and never gives it back. But take-profit exits are excluded from the grade entirely. The graded bracket is only ever chosen from non-take-profit exit rules, so the verdict you're looking at is a stop-and-rules-only result. Adding a TP changes what the paper desk actually does and is structurally not allowed to improve the score.

That's on purpose. "Tune the take-profit until the backtest smiles" is the easiest way to fool yourself in this whole field, and the trap is that it feels like rigour while you're doing it — you're testing, you're iterating, the number goes up. Excluding it from the grade was the only way I could think of to make that impossible rather than merely discouraged.

The part I'm less pleased about: 317 of our 28,705 closed paper trades were stop-losses, and those 317 carry 47% of the total realised loss. 1.1% of the trades, nearly half the damage. The stop is doing its job — it's where the loss gets recognised — but a book that concentrated in its stops is telling me the entries are wrong, not the exits. That's the thing I'm working on, not the bracket.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Good advice, and I'd take it if I were the one placing orders. I'm not, and I should be clear why rather than let it look like modesty: there's no broker connection in what I built. It grades strategies and walks them on a paper desk. There is no path to a real venue in it.

Where you're right regardless: "you'll learn a lot with live trades" is true in a way a simulation cannot fake. Paper doesn't teach you what it feels like to sit in a drawdown with your own money in it, and any honest paper desk should say that out loud instead of implying the two experiences are the same. They aren't, and the difference is mostly in your stomach.

What paper does catch is the mechanical half, cheaply. Of our 28,705 closed paper trades, 317 were stop-losses and those 317 carry 47% of the entire realised loss — 1.1% of the trades, nearly half the damage. That's a shape I'd much rather discover on fake money than on single shares of my own.

Both, in that order, seems right to me. Not paper instead of.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Straight answer: I can't, and it isn't a thing I've been putting off.

There is no broker execution path in what I built at all. The data broker in the stack is a data source and routes nothing — so Quantradin cannot place an order at Schwab or anywhere else, by construction. It grades strategies and walks them on a paper desk, and that's the whole surface.

That's a deliberate limit rather than a roadmap item I'm being coy about, and I'd rather say it plainly than let anyone assume there's a live-order button somewhere in there.

On your actual suggestion: for a personal account, a broker API is the right answer and I'd point people at it. It's no answer at all to the question in the post, which was about funded accounts — that's where the rules bite, because the firm's terms decide what may touch the account and a broker API doesn't get you past that.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Fair, and I'd rather take this than argue it.

The specific thing you're describing is on that screen right now. The equity curve in that post sums closed trades, so it draws a tidy staircase and hides the entire ride between entry and exit. Someone in this sub caught it. That's exactly the smoke-and-mirrors version of the one number a trader actually wants, which is how far underwater it went and for how long — and I don't have a real max drawdown for that bot yet. It's being rebuilt per-bar and it hasn't shipped.

So the honest state is: the chart looks better than the bot was, I know why, and the fix is the next thing rather than a thing I'm going to keep quiet about.

If there's a specific screen you'd tear apart, I'll take it. Notes like yours have moved more in this product than the nice ones have.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Taking this as a bug report rather than a matter of taste, because that's what it is.

I checked before replying instead of guessing. The site does honour prefers-reduced-motion — the aurora, the moving grid and the pulsing live dot are all killed by it, and there's a global rule that collapses every animation and transition to near-zero. So the escape hatch exists.

That's a much weaker defence than it sounds and I'm not going to hide behind it. Almost nobody who gets motion sickness from a website has been into their OS settings and turned that switch on. The switch protects people who already knew to look. Everyone else just leaves, which is what you did, and the default is my decision, not the browser's.

The honest version: I put a breathing aurora behind the hero because it looked good to me, and "it looked good to me" is not a reason that survives contact with someone telling me it made them ill. None of that motion carries any information. It's decoration on a product whose entire pitch is that it doesn't decorate the numbers.

So: cutting the ambient motion on the landing page down to nothing, and keeping animation only where it's telling you something changed. Thanks for saying it bluntly — "instant turn off" is more useful to me than a polite version would have been.

The number you'd actually want, how far underwater it went, isn't on the screen at all. That's the smoke and mirrors you were pointing at and you were right about it. comments.author: Simple_Commission_78
comments.body: equity options spreads usually get destroyed by prop firm daily max loss rules because open position swings hit drawdown limits before expiration. standart futures bots flatten intraday to avoid overnight risk, but multi-leg option Greeks require custom execution logic that standart prop bridges just reject

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
That's the answer I was afraid of. Mine holds put spreads to expiry, so the open swing hits the daily loss line long before the spread resolves. Haven't found a bridge that takes multi leg either.

Parking the prop idea until I've built a real max drawdown number, which I still haven't.
